transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Thanks for seeing me. Well, it's... it's kind of embarrassing to talk about, to be honest, but the main reason I’m here is that I just keep getting up when I'm absolutely supposed to stay put. Like, I literally cannot stay in my chair. 

I’m a private investigator, which sounds really action-packed, but honestly, a huge part of the job is just sitting across a desk doing long intake interviews with clients who are usually very stressed out. And lately, right in the middle of them pouring their hearts out about a sensitive surveillance case or whatever it might be, I just stand up. I don't even fully realize I'm doing it until I'm pacing around the office or staring out the window, and they're looking at me like I'm completely ignoring them. 

And it’s bleeding into everything else, too. I do some tutoring on the side to make extra money, and I can't even sit through a basic one-hour session with a student without popping up to walk around the table or fiddle with the whiteboard. Even at my book club! Which is supposed to be relaxing, you know, we just drink wine and talk about historical fiction. Everyone else is perfectly happy lounging on the sofa for two hours, but I’m constantly up and down, going to the kitchen, standing by the mantel... 

It's just getting to the point where people are really starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen. My friends, my clients, they're all giving me these looks. It’s incredibly unprofessional at work, and socially it just makes me look rude, but I just have this overwhelming urge to get out of my seat.
Are you currently taking any medications, especially any antipsychotic or anti-nausea drugs, or have you started or changed any medication recently?

No, no, nothing like that. I don’t take any medications at all, actually. I mean, I’ll take an ibuprofen if I have a really bad headache from staring at surveillance footage for too long—which, honestly, happens way more often than you’d think when you’re squinting at a monitor trying to read a blurry license plate at two in the morning—but as for actual daily prescriptions? Or antipsychotics or anti-nausea pills? Not a single one. 

I haven’t started anything new, and I haven’t changed anything, mostly because there’s absolutely nothing to change. I’ve always been one of those people who tries to avoid taking pills if I can possibly help it. I just feel like, especially with my line of work, I really need to have a completely clear head, you know? If I’m staking out a location or trying to catch a tiny discrepancy in a client's story during an intake, I just can’t afford to be groggy or deal with any weird side effects that might throw me off my game. 

So yeah, my medicine cabinet is basically just toothpaste, some loose bandaids, and maybe a bottle of vitamin C that probably expired back in 2019. I don't even take a daily multivitamin because I can never remember to take it at the same time every day anyway. So, no, definitely no medications.
Thinking back, did you have this same kind of restlessness and trouble staying seated as a child or teenager, or is this something that's really only started recently?

Oh, wow, no, this is definitely not a new thing. Not at all. If anything, it's just that it's becoming more of a problem now because of the expectations of my job and, you know, being a grown adult. But as a kid? Oh my gosh, it was constant. 

I actually found a box of my old report cards recently—I was helping my mom clean out her attic, which is a whole other story, she has so much stuff up there—but anyway, I was looking through them, and it was almost comical. Every single teacher, from first grade all the way through middle school, wrote the exact same thing. "Bright student, but refuses to stay in her seat." Or "Needs constant reminders to sit down." Or "Interrupts and struggles to wait her turn." It was like they were all copying off each other! 

My mother still jokes about it. She always says that I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through, looking for clues, because I literally could not just sit at a desk. I was always the kid volunteering to erase the chalkboard, or hand out papers, or run messages to the office—anything, absolutely anything, just to have an excuse to be up and moving. 

And in high school, it wasn't much better. I managed to channel some of it into sports, I ran track, which helped burn off the energy, but sitting through a double period of AP History? Torture. Absolute torture. I would constantly ask to go to the bathroom just so I could walk the halls for five minutes. 

So, yeah, this feeling, this absolute need to be up and moving around, it’s been with me my entire life. It’s just that when you’re a kid, people kind of write it off as you being a tomboy or just having a lot of energy. But now that I’m forty-nine and trying to run a serious investigation business, the whole "pacing the room like a caged tiger" routine isn't quite as charming.
